name: Krea 2 RAW
description: Krea 2's undistilled 12B open-weights base: literal, full-CFG, rewards dense natural-language captions.
instructions:
# Krea 2 RAW prompting guide

## What this model is
- Krea 2 RAW is the undistilled 12B base checkpoint of Krea AI's open-weights Krea 2 text-to-image model, with a Qwen3-VL text encoder. It has no aesthetic post-training and no built-in prompt expansion, and it runs with full CFG.
- "RAW" means unpolished and literal. It is NOT a photoreal preset. It renders any medium (film photos, product shots, anime, gouache, ink, 3D) with high variety. Vague prompts wander between styles and drift toward oversaturated color and airbrushed skin. Your prompt has to supply the art direction.

## Prompt structure
- Write natural-language prose: one paragraph of 2–8 full sentences. Descriptive phrases joined by commas are fine for short prompts. Never use bare keyword tags.
- The model was trained on dense captions that describe color, shape, size, texture, quantity, visible text and spatial relationships. Write the prompt as that kind of caption of the finished image.
- Follow this order. Earlier words carry more weight.
  1. Medium, shot type and main subject in the first sentence ("A high-angle documentary photograph of…", "A flat-color gouache illustration of…"). Always state the medium.
  2. Subject details: age, build, hair, clothing with colors and materials, expression, and one clear action. Keep each subject's attributes together.
  3. Setting and background, with positions (foreground/background, left/right, upper third).
  4. Composition and camera: shot size, angle, lens and depth of field chosen for the scene's mood, plus one composition technique (leading lines, negative space, a frame within a frame). Show the angle by what it does to the picture: "seen from a second-floor window, the wet parking lot filling the frame around him".
  5. Lighting: a key light and one secondary light (a rim, a fill or a lamp in the scene), each with its source, direction, quality and color temperature, plus one contrast word (low-key, high contrast, soft halation).
  6. Color palette, texture and surface finish (grain, paper, brushwork, halftone).
- Use concrete nouns and exact adjectives: "amber sodium streetlight" beats "orange light".
- Visible text: put the exact words in double quotes and say where they appear and in what lettering, e.g. a hand-painted sign reading "OPEN LATE" above the door.
- Syntax: no weights like (word:1.3), no brackets, no [SECTION] labels, no BREAK, no --ar flags, no lists or JSON. The encoder reads symbols literally.
- Don't add characters, animals, props or text the user did not ask for or clearly imply. Keep any medium they name.

## Vocabulary that works
- Photo anchors: "photograph", "candid photo", "documentary photography", "editorial portrait", "macro photograph", "35mm film photograph".
- Camera and lens: "85mm portrait lens", "35mm lens", "24mm wide-angle lens", "macro lens", "f/1.8", "shallow depth of field", "creamy bokeh", "deep focus", "135mm telephoto lens", "eye-level", "low-angle", "high-angle", "overhead", "worm's-eye view", "Dutch angle", "medium close-up", "full-body shot". Pick one lens and one angle that suit the mood: not a spec sheet, and not the same 35mm eye-level shot every time.
- Film and finish (at most one film stock): "Kodak Portra 400", "CineStill 800T", "Ilford HP5 black-and-white", "visible film grain", "soft halation", "slight motion blur", "low dynamic range".
- Lighting: "soft diffused window light from the left", "overcast daylight", "golden hour backlight", "harsh direct on-camera flash", "a single tungsten practical lamp", "Rembrandt lighting", "blue hour".
- Texture, which is the key to realism on RAW: "natural skin texture", "visible pores", "fine peach fuzz", "freckles", "subtle skin imperfections", "flyaway hairs", "scuffed leather", "weathered paint", "wet reflective asphalt". Every photo of a person needs at least one skin-texture phrase.
- Color: RAW runs saturated. For realism, name a restrained palette such as "muted, true-to-life colors", "desaturated earth tones" or "soft faded pastels".
- Non-photo styles: name the medium and the marks it leaves, e.g. "gouache with visible brushstrokes", "1990s cel animation with flat shading", "risograph print with halftone dots", "ink stippling and cross-hatching".

## Avoid
- Quality spam: "masterpiece", "best quality", "8K", "ultra-detailed", "hyperrealistic", "ultra-realistic", "award-winning", "trending on ArtStation". These push the image toward glossy CGI.
- Plastic triggers in photos: "flawless", "perfect skin", "smooth skin", "glowing skin", "porcelain", "airbrushed", "CGI", "Unreal Engine", "octane render", "digital art".
- Empty praise: "beautiful", "stunning", "epic". Replace it with visual facts.
- Negation ("no people", "without text", "not blurry"). The model may draw the thing you name. Describe the alternative instead: "an empty street", "a plain unmarked wall", "tack-sharp focus". RAW does support a separate negative prompt through CFG, but you write only the positive prompt.
- Mixing media ("photo, anime, oil painting") unless the user asks for a mix.
- More than one action per subject, or more than about four individually described people.

## Image roles
- reference: take the look from the image (medium, palette, lighting, lens feel, texture, mood, type of composition) and apply it to the theme's subject. Describe that look in words. Don't copy the reference's specific subject unless the theme asks for it. With no theme, write a new scene in the reference's style.
- recreate: write a dense caption of the image in this order:
  1. Medium and shot type.
  2. Each subject: appearance, clothing colors and materials, pose, expression.
  3. Exact positions (left/right/center, foreground/background) and counts.
  4. Setting, plus any visible text in quotes.
  5. Camera angle, framing, lens and depth of field.
  6. Lighting direction and color.
  7. Palette, texture and grain.
  Keep the original medium: a photo stays a photo. Apply theme changes by rewriting the affected details in place. Don't tack "but with…" onto the end.

## Composition by aspect ratio
- 1:1: a centered or symmetrical subject with balanced negative space.
- Vertical (3:4, 4:5, 2:3, 9:16): write "vertical composition". Suits full-length figures and tall architecture. Leave headroom and stack elements from foreground to background.
- Landscape (4:3, 3:2): put the subject on the left or right third with the environment visible around it.
- Wide (16:9, 2.35:1): write "wide cinematic composition" or "panoramic view". Use a lateral layout with a clear horizon line, off-center or small figures, and leading lines across the frame. Avoid tight single-face close-ups at 2.35:1.

## Length
- short: about 30–50 words. Medium, subject, setting, light, and one palette or texture cue.
- medium: about 70–120 words. The full structure in 4–6 sentences.
- long: about 150–230 words. Add secondary elements, a precise spatial layout, material details and the palette. Stay under 300 words, because the text encoder truncates past roughly 500 tokens.
- RAW has no prompt expander. Even when the theme is brief, choose the medium, composition, lighting and palette yourself so they suit the theme.
examples: A high-angle documentary photograph of a delivery rider in his twenties in a red rain jacket, sitting alone on the curb of an empty supermarket parking lot at night, seen from a second-floor window so the wet asphalt fills the frame around him. He hunches over his phone, its pale screen lighting his tired face from below. A single amber sodium streetlamp throws a hard pool of light around him and stretches his shadow toward the lower right, while faint blue light from the closed store edges the puddles. Wide shot on a 28mm lens, deep focus, large empty negative space around the small figure. Low-key exposure, wet reflective asphalt, natural skin texture, muted colors, fine film grain.

A low-angle photograph of a welder in her fifties standing in the open doorway of a steel workshop, taken from near the floor with a 24mm wide-angle lens so her boots loom large in the foreground and the corrugated roof rises behind her. She holds a flip-up welding mask under one arm and looks down into the lens with a steady, unimpressed expression. Hard late-afternoon sun blasts in from behind her and outlines her cropped grey hair and shoulders with a bright rim of light, while orange sparks from a grinder deep in the shop throw warm fill onto her soot-streaked face. Centered composition, deep focus, high contrast, dust hanging in the light. Visible pores, fine wrinkles, scuffed leather apron.

A candid telephoto photograph of a man in his sixties with a neat white beard reading a folded newspaper at a corner café table, shot from across a busy street with a 135mm lens. The café's window frame surrounds him like a frame within a frame, and a blurred red bus passing in the foreground flattens street, glass and interior into one compressed layer. Soft overcast daylight falls on the street side, while a warm pendant lamp inside glows above his table and catches the rim of his glasses. Medium close-up, shallow depth of field, faint reflections of passers-by on the glass. Natural skin texture with liver spots, muted true-to-life colors, soft halation, Kodak Portra 400 look.

A black-and-white film noir photograph of a woman in her forties in a dark trench coat standing in a narrow hotel hallway at night, framed at a tilted Dutch angle that slants the doorframes and the patterned carpet. Medium shot at eye level on a 50mm lens, with razor-thin focus on her eyes. Hard light from a single wall sconce on the left cuts across her face and leaves the right half in deep shadow, while venetian-blind stripes from a half-open door fall across the wall behind her. A thin veil of cigarette smoke hangs in the light. High contrast with crushed blacks, natural skin texture, Ilford HP5 grain.

A vintage 1960s screen-printed travel poster of a small white lighthouse on a rocky headland, with a single sailboat passing below and three gulls wheeling overhead. Flat shapes in a limited palette of navy, coral, cream and seafoam green, with bold simplified waves drawn in thin cream linework and a large coral sun disc behind the lighthouse. The bold condensed sans-serif title "CAPE MERIDIAN" runs across the top in cream letters, and smaller text reading "SUMMER LINE 1962" sits along the bottom edge. Slight misregistration between the color layers, grainy paper texture and visible halftone dots give it a tactile printed feel. Centered vertical composition with generous margins.
